title: End-Use Census With Error Bars
problem: Load research gets appliance counts from small samples and surveys, and the forecast takes those counts at face value. The meters in this pipeline already show the counts are uncertain. Electric heat comes out anywhere from 2,873 to 4,143 homes depending on the threshold. The heat pump classifier reaches only 0.718 AUC. Half the EV list never charges at home. Nobody can say how wide the error is on the inventory that sets when this system turns winter-peaking.
solution: The tool runs on the classifier scores the pipeline already produces, the partial EV and heat pump lists (the challenge says each holds about 25% of likely owners), the full solar list, and hourly weather. Step one corrects the raw counts using the lists: it estimates how often each class detector finds a true owner, using a positive-unlabeled class-prior method (the existing EV estimate of about 560 is the same idea). The output is an inventory per end use with bootstrap 90% intervals, not a single count. Step two builds a weather-normalized load shape for each end use. It subtracts matched homes without the appliance from homes with it, so each end use gets a kW figure at the summer and winter event hours. Step three sizes the uncertainty on when the system flips to winter peaking, then picks the smallest set of homes to verify by survey or site visit that would narrow the intervals most, using Neyman allocation across score bands. Load research, forecasting and program design would use the inventory, the per-end-use kW at peak and the verification list in their next forecast cycle.
decision_changed: Two decisions change. First, the end-use saturation numbers and kW-at-peak figures that go into Avangrid's residential load forecast become calibrated ranges with error bars, replacing point counts or survey numbers. Second, load research's survey or metering budget moves from random sampling to the specific homes the tool picks, the ones whose verification narrows the winter-peak crossover range most. The planning question changes from "do we turn winter-peaking at about 5,100 more electric-heat conversions?" to "the crossover falls between X and Y conversions, and verifying these N homes cuts that range by Z."
evidence: Electric heat inventory ranges from 2,873 to 4,143 homes depending on the threshold (class.electric_heat.sensitivity_low / sensitivity_high), so today's count carries about a 44% swing

About 5,100 more conversions at 3.29 kW each would make the system winter-peaking (insight.homes_to_flip_winter_peaking; insight.heat_conversion_added_kw_at_winter_peak). The inventory's uncertainty therefore moves the crossover date directly.

Heat pump detection is weak: PU AUC 0.718, held-out recall 16.7%, confidence 'low: listed HP homes and resistance homes share one kW-vs-temperature curve' (class.heat_pump.pu_auc, recall_heldout, confidence). Weather adds 4.2 AUC points (class.weather_gain.heat_pump_auc_points).

The EV list implies about 560 EV homes in the data (class.ev.implied_total), but only 30.7% of listed EVs show home Level 2 charging (class.ev.recall_heldout) and 51.4% show none (class.ev.labeled_no_home_l2_pct). Raw counts and the true inventory can differ widely.

Benchmark: NREL 2024's AMI classifier with ResStock matching reports 16.6% median monthly CV-RMSE (checks/citations.yaml). The label lists are 'about 25% of the total likely' EV and heat pump customers (Challenge Statement.pdf, Data Provided).
build_plan_24h: Team of three, with features frozen at hour 16. Person A, hours 0 to 10: an inventory module on top of the existing per-class scores. It estimates detection rates from the EV, heat pump and solar lists (Elkan-Noto style). It corrects counts per class, bootstraps 90% intervals over homes, and writes the results to facts.json under new inventory.* keys so the self-checking repo still traces every number. Person B, hours 0 to 12: per-end-use load shapes. For each detected class, it computes the hourly difference by month between class homes and non-class homes matched on annual kWh decile and weather. It reports kW per unit at the summer (16:00-20:00) and winter (17:00-21:00) event windows and checks the result against the existing 3.29 kW per heat conversion. Person C, hours 0 to 8: the verification sample designer. It applies Neyman allocation across classifier score bands to choose the N homes that most narrow the electric heat and heat pump intervals, and outputs the interval width before and after verifying them. Hours 8 to 16: Person C turns the electric-heat interval into a range for the winter crossover. Hours 16 to 24, all three: three deck slides (inventory with error bars, end-use kW at peak, sample plan and crossover range), a limitations line on the list-bias assumption, and a re-run of the repo checks. Cut order if behind: crossover range first, then non-heat end-use shapes, then reducing the sample designer to a ranked list.
biggest_risk: The correction assumes the label lists are a random sample of true owners, and they are not. 51.4% of listed EVs show no home Level 2 charging, so the EV list mixes home chargers with people who charge away from home. A list-based detection rate would then inflate the corrected inventory. A rigorous judge could also call the intervals false precision. The mitigation is to say this on the slide, show the correction both with and without the list-bias adjustment, and lean on electric heat and solar, where the evidence is strongest. A second risk: it is less flashy than a battery story, so it has to be pitched as making the battery and forecast numbers trustworthy, not as a replacement for them.

title: Battery Eligibility Rulebook Simulator
problem: The current battery list gives two IQ 10C units to every one of the 4,079 homes that peak hardest. On assumed prices that pays back in 23 to 33 years against a 15-year warranty, so a regulator would not approve it. The battery earns its keep somewhere else: it lets a home add an EV charger or heat pump without a service upgrade. The program's eligibility rules should target that job, and sometimes one unit is enough instead of two.
solution: This adds a policy-rule layer on top of the existing classifier, segment, and BESS outputs (customer_classes.csv, bess_candidates.csv, the 3 kVA headroom test). The inputs are each home's classes, segment, event-hour load, and the load it is likely to add next: a detected unlisted Level 2 charger, electric heat, or an emerging heat-pump prospect. The policy manager writes eligibility rules as editable criteria, for example "exclude seasonal homes", "require a pending electrification load that fails 3 kVA", "one unit if one passes 3 kVA, otherwise two" and "solar homes first". The engine scores each home on a value stack: event-hour MW, TOU shift, and an avoided service upgrade, which stays a flagged assumption until someone supplies a sourced cost. The output is a budget-capped funded list with units per home, and a side-by-side table of homes, units, MW, capex and payback under each rulebook. Avangrid's storage policy and customer programs staff would use the table to decide the eligibility language in a NY BTM storage program proposal, and the ranked list would go to field outreach.
decision_changed: The decision is BTM battery program eligibility and unit allocation. Today's rule is "persistent peakers get two units". The new rule is "homes adding load that breaks the 3 kVA rule, sized at one unit where one passes". That turns the battery from a capacity resource that does not pay back into a non-wires alternative to service upgrades, and it gives the regulatory filing a stated, defensible answer to who gets a battery and why.
evidence: Payback is 23 to 33 years on assumed prices (bess.simple_payback_low_yr = 23.0, bess.simple_payback_high_yr = 33.0) against a 15-year program warranty (Challenge Statement, BESS spec table)

An unmanaged Level 2 EV fails the 3 kVA rule at 99.3% of homes without a battery. One IQ 10C fixes 56.6% and two fix 100% (bess.headroom_rule.ev_fail_pct_none, ev_pass_pct_one_unit, ev_pass_pct_two_units)
Every candidate is sized at two units today: 4,079 homes, 8,158 units, $73.4M to $106.1M capex (bess.size.two_units, bess.units_total, bess.capex_low_usd_m, bess.capex_high_usd_m)
Returns fall as more homes are added: the top 1,000 homes give 2.72 MW in summer and all 4,079 give 14.86 MW (bess.supply_curve.top1000_summer_mw, bess.capacity_relief_mw)

Already-electrified peakers are a separate tier: 1,491 homes giving 4.4 MW summer and 5.98 MW winter. Meanwhile 392 Level 2 chargers are missing from the EV list (bess.tier.T1_electrified_peaker.*, class.ev.l2_unlisted)
build_plan_24h: Person A (data, about 10 h): join customer_classes.csv, the segment table and bess_candidates.csv into one per-home table. Add a per-home "next load" field (unlisted L2, electric heat conversion, emerging heat-pump prospect) and that home's 3 kVA result at 0, 1 and 2 units, reusing the existing headroom functions. Add the units-needed calculation so one-unit homes show up. Person B (rules engine, about 10 h): write a small YAML rulebook format and an evaluator that applies the criteria, assigns units, computes the value stack, and returns a funded list under a dollar or MW cap. Add three preset rulebooks (Peaker, which is today's rule; Electrification Gate; Solar First) and write each result to facts.json so the repo's self-check covers the slide numbers. Person C (deck and assumptions, about 10 h): look for a sourced avoided service-upgrade cost and NY capacity value to replace the placeholders, and leave them labeled as assumptions if none is found. Build two or three slides: rulebook comparison table, supply curve per rulebook, one-vs-two unit split. Run make check.
biggest_risk: The pitch says batteries pay back by avoiding service upgrades, but the brief has no avoided-upgrade cost and no transformer or feeder mapping. Unless a sourced $/upgrade value turns up, the winning rulebook rests on one new assumption, and the judges could see it as moving the payback problem rather than solving it. The 3 kVA test is also optimistic on hourly data, as the readout notes for 15-minute intervals.

title: Next-Best-Offer Program Router
problem: Avangrid's program managers can see who has an AC, an EV or electric heat, but nothing tells them which single offer each home should get next quarter or what each delivered kW costs. So battery money risks going to plain peak relief, which the pipeline shows does not pay back (23 to 33 years against a 15-year warranty), while cheaper offers sit unused and half the EV list gets mistargeted.
solution: Inputs: the pipeline's per-customer outputs (customer_classes.csv, segments, bess_candidates.csv, the 3 kVA headroom test) plus one assumptions file with program cost per participant, incentive and uptake rate, every value tagged assumption.* the way facts.json already does. Method: score each home against five offers (smart-thermostat DR, managed EV charging plus an EV TOU rate, battery as an electrification enabler where the home fails the 3 kVA rule, heat-pump marketing to the emerging segment, a pool-pump timer). Each home x offer pair gets its expected coincident kW at the summer and winter event hours and its cost per kW. Seasonal and inactive meters are excluded. A greedy portfolio fill gives each home at most one offer, cheapest $/kW first, until a MW target or a budget is reached. Output: one program supply curve (MW against $ across all offers) and one launch-ready campaign list per program (customer ID, offer, expected kW, confidence, reason code). The Customer Programs manager uses it to size next quarter's enrollment campaigns; Load Research and Forecasting use the same curve to book expected MW.
decision_changed: It changes who gets which program offer next quarter and where the battery budget goes. Summer peak relief goes to thermostats first. Batteries are reserved for homes where they let an EV or heat pump connect without a service study. Unlisted Level 2 chargers get managed-charging offers instead of the stale EV list. Seasonal homes are dropped from every campaign. Today each program targets its own list on its own; after this, Avangrid can commit to one MW target and fund it at the lowest cost per kW.

bess.simple_payback_low_yr = 23 and bess.simple_payback_high_yr = 33 years against the 15-year program warranty (Challenge Statement): batteries cannot be the default peak offer

bess.headroom_rule.ev_fail_pct_none = 99.3% of homes fail the 3 kVA rule with an unmanaged Level 2 charger; bess.headroom_rule.ev_pass_pct_two_units = 100% pass with the program battery: where the battery offer belongs

class.ev.labeled_no_home_l2_pct = 51.4% of listed EVs show no home Level 2 charging, while class.ev.l2_unlisted = 392 homes charge at Level 2 off-list: managed-charging targeting from the meters, not the list
ACEEE 2020 (checks/citations.yaml): targeting on AMI features, the top half saved 'nearly 3.5 times more'; seg.seasonal.count = 2455 homes (9.6%) are excluded from every campaign
build_plan_24h: Hours 0 to 2 (all three): freeze the offer schema (customer_id, offer, kw_summer, kw_winter, cost_usd, confidence, reason) and the assumptions file with labeled placeholder costs and uptake. Person A, hours 2 to 12: per-offer eligibility and kW in analysis/offers.py, reusing the existing features. Thermostat kW = each home's AC weather load x the shed assumption. Managed EV kW = the Level 2 block overlapping event hours. Battery-as-enabler = homes that fail the 3 kVA rule alone and pass with the battery. HP marketing = the emerging segment. Pool timer = pool class daytime floor. Person B, hours 2 to 14: the portfolio fill in analysis/portfolio.py (one offer per home, $/kW ranking, MW or budget target), a +/-50% sensitivity on cost and uptake, campaign CSVs per program, and every new number written to facts.json so the self-check still passes. Person C, hours 2 to 16: four slides (the offer matrix by segment, the cross-program supply curve, a one-page campaign card for next quarter, and a [NET] row with program cost vs capacity value plus payback), plus the 'scales to millions' note (vectorized per customer, about 20 s ingest today). Hours 16 to 24: freeze, run make check, blind-read the deck against the rubric, and cut in order: pool timer first, then HP marketing, then winter sensitivity.
biggest_risk: The data contains no program cost, incentive or uptake rate. The $/kW ranking that orders the whole portfolio therefore rests on placeholder assumptions, and the Customer Programs judge knows the real numbers and may see the ranking as invented. Mitigations: every assumption is labeled on the slide, a sensitivity band shows which rankings hold when costs move +/-50%, and the deck says plainly that Avangrid's own program costs drop into one file to rerun. A second risk is that it looks like a repackage of segments the pipeline already has, so the supply curve has to carry the new insight visibly.

title: Winter Flip Forecaster
problem: Avangrid's capacity plans and program targeting assume this system peaks on summer afternoons, yet the meters show each gas-to-electric heat conversion adds about 3.3 kW at the winter peak, and only about 5,100 more conversions would make the system winter-peaking. Today's EV and heat-pump lists cannot warn planners of that flip, because the lists miss most of what the meters see.
solution: The tool is a bottom-up electrification scenario engine built on the existing pipeline. It starts from each home's measured 8,760-hour profile, its Part 1 class probabilities and its fitted kW-per-degree response. For each scenario it adds hourly change profiles to every home, sums them back to a system load for each hour, and recomputes the summer and winter top-100-hour peaks. The scenarios set the number of heat-pump conversions (taken first from the 'emerging' segment, which already owns cooling, so its summer AC load is netted out), Level 2 chargers (managed or unmanaged) and battery or thermostat placements. The output is a curve from adoption to peak, which marks the conversion count where winter overtakes summer. It also shows how many MW each lever (managed charging, winter battery dispatch, thermostat setback) buys back, and which segments carry the new winter peak. The load forecasting and load research teams use it to pick the season they plan capacity around. The program team uses the same run to rank batteries for the peak the system will have.
decision_changed: The tool changes which peak the battery and DR programs are ranked against, and when distribution planning starts treating winter as the binding season. Today's ranking favors summer grid peakers: the T3 tier gives 10.43 MW in summer but only 5.33 MW in winter. Once the curve shows the winter crossover is near, the program should reorder toward the T1 electrified peakers, which give 5.98 MW in winter against 4.4 MW in summer, and should pair heat-pump marketing with winter dispatch and managed charging. Planners get a trigger to watch: the count of conversions measured on the meters, compared against the flip threshold. That replaces relying on list-based adoption counts.
evidence: insight.homes_to_flip_winter_peaking = 5100 homes (19.9% of homes, insight.share_to_flip_winter_peaking_pct); insight.summer_minus_winter_mw = 16.8 MW gap between 59.4 MW summer and 42.6 MW winter peak
insight.heat_conversion_added_kw_at_winter_peak = 3.29 kW per home; insight.electric_heat_winter_peak_share_pct = 31.9% of winter top-100h load from 11.2% of homes
bess.tier.T1_electrified_peaker winter_mw 5.98 vs summer_mw 4.4; bess.tier.T3_grid_peaker summer_mw 10.43 vs winter_mw 5.33: the best battery ranking depends on which season binds
class.ev.labeled_no_home_l2_pct = 51.4% of listed EVs show no home L2, while class.ev.l2_unlisted = 392 homes charge at L2 off-list: list-based adoption counts are wrong in both directions
RMI 2025 (checks/citations.yaml): utility 2035 demand forecasts up 'over 20 percent', with overbuilding costing almost $2 billion: a bottom-up, meter-calibrated forecast is the guard against that
build_plan_24h: Person 1, about 8 hours, scenario engine. Write a function that takes the 25,653 x 8,760 matrix plus a scenario and returns system hourly load. It builds the heat-pump change from the existing per-home heating response (hp_kw_per_degf 0.051, 3.06 kW at 0F), minus the converted home's AC load in summer. It reuses the existing L2 block shape for EVs, both unmanaged and shifted to after 23:00, and the existing battery dispatch for the summer and winter windows. Self-check: a zero-adoption run must reproduce 59.4 MW and 42.6 MW exactly, enforced in make check. Person 2, about 8 hours, sweep and uncertainty. Sweep conversions from 0 to 8,000 in steps of 250. Repeat the sweep using the electric-heat range (2,873 to 4,143 homes) and using the heat-pump-versus-resistance mix as bounds, which gives a band around the flip point rather than one number. Then rerun the battery ranking with winter-weighted relief and write the new numbers into facts.json. Person 3, about 8 hours, deck. Three slides: (1) the adoption-to-peak curve with the crossover band; (2) MW bought back per lever; (3) the equations, the self-check, and a 'what to plug in' box for Avangrid's own adoption rates. Then run make check DECK=deck.pptx so every number traces back to code.
biggest_risk: The tool turns adoption counts into peak MW, but nothing in the data says how fast adoption will happen or which gas homes will convert, so it cannot honestly print a year. Without Avangrid's adoption forecast it can only give a threshold. The per-conversion kW also comes from a heat-pump and resistance curve the classifier cannot separate (heat pump AUC 0.718), and the 10,072 missing customers mean the MW figures describe 25,653 homes, not the service territory. Judges may also read it as a restatement of the existing 5,100-home number unless the deck shows the uncertainty band and the reordered battery ranking.

title: Monthly New-Load Watch Feed
problem: The pipeline is a one-time yearly study. At Avangrid's 3 million-plus customers, its inventory starts going stale on day one: a new EV charger or a converted electric-heat home that appears next month goes unseen until someone reruns the study. A silent input defect like the repeated zip, which dropped 10,072 of 35,725 customers, would also pass unnoticed.
solution: Rebuild the existing pipeline as an incremental monthly job. Each month it reads that month's AMI and weather data, partitioned by month and customer shard. It updates rolling 12-month features and reruns the existing rules and positive-unlabeled models only on homes whose load shape changed. Before any classification it runs a data-quality contract: row counts against the customer roster, a content hash that flags a duplicated file (this check would have caught the 10,072 missing customers), gaps in timestamps, and coverage by zip. The output is a monthly change feed with one row per home that changed: a new Level 2 charger, a new electric-heat signature, a new solar home, or a change in battery-candidate rank and 3 kVA headroom status. A running winter-flip counter tracks progress toward the roughly 5,100 conversions that would make the system winter-peaking. Distribution planners and load forecasters read the feed, Customer Programs uses it to trigger outreach (managed charging, battery offers), and the Data Engineer runs the pipeline with drift alerts on recall for the labeled lists.
decision_changed: The change is to when and how Avangrid refreshes its customer-technology inventory and its program targeting. Today that work is a periodic study, and the EV and heat-pump lists rely on what customers report. Under this tool it becomes a monthly feed. Two decisions move. First, distribution planning and forecasting get a dated alert when a home's load signature shows a new Level 2 charger or electric heat, instead of learning about it after an overload. Second, Customer Programs gets the battery and managed-charging offer to a home while it is still deciding to electrify, which is when the battery-as-upgrade-avoider case is strongest. Load forecasting also gets a measured monthly count toward the winter-peaking flip point to replace an assumed one.
evidence: data.rows_read = 223,319,163 hourly readings, scale.ingest_seconds = 18.6 s, scale.matrix_gb = 1.25 GB (facts.json): the measured baseline. Scaling linearly to 3M customers (brief: 'over 3 million customers') gives about 117x, so roughly 36 min of ingest and about 146 GB. That extrapolation is my arithmetic, not a measured fact, and the build has to measure it.
data.customers_missing = 10,072 of data.customers_promised = 35,725 (facts.json): one repeated zip silently removed 28% of customers. This is the defect the data-quality contract is built to catch.

If the slides read as architecture boxes, it earns little of the 40% for business value, and scalability is just one bullet inside the 10% Innovation criterion. The heat and cooling rules need a full season of weather to fit their slopes, so monthly reclassification on partial windows may flag noisy changes. The deck has to say that out loud and show that early-month flags settle by the end of the season.

title: Hidden Load Register
problem: Distribution assets are sized from what the utility's records say is behind each meter, but the meters show large loads the records miss: 392 Level 2 chargers not on the EV list and electric heat in about 1 in 9 homes, mostly unlisted. Overload risk builds up wherever these unrecorded loads cluster, and an overload is usually found only when an asset fails.
solution: Inputs: the pipeline's existing per-customer classes and probabilities, the utility's EV, heat-pump and solar lists, hourly AMI and weather, plus an optional meter-to-transformer CSV with a published schema. Method: for each meter, compare detected loads with recorded loads. Price each unrecorded load in kW at the system's coincident peaks: Level 2 block size at the summer event hours, and the heating slope taken to the 2.1F winter peak. Run the 3 kVA service test on the result. Then roll it up to whatever grouping is supplied (transformer, feeder or zip), so each asset gets recorded load plus hidden load. Output: a ranked hidden_loads.csv and an asset stress table that shows, for each flagged home, whether a battery, managed charging or a field check removes the overage. Users: reliability and distribution planning for inspection and upgrade order, and the battery program for picking sites where a battery defers an upgrade.
decision_changed: It changes how Avangrid orders transformer and service inspections and upgrades, and how it sites batteries. Today both follow recorded load and failures. With the register, they follow metered hidden load at peak, ranked before anything fails. It also shifts where batteries pay: the readout already shows they do not pay back on capacity and TOU value alone, so the register points them at homes where they avoid an upgrade.

bess.headroom_rule.ev_fail_pct_none = 99.3% of homes without an EV break the 3 kVA rule with an unmanaged Level 2; one IQ 10C fixes 56.6%, two fix 100% (facts.json)
DOE AMI report 2019: 'three customers buy a Tesla' and transformer load triples; SMUD: up to 17% of transformers may need upgrades from EVs (brief, checks/citations.yaml)

For each meter, compute detected minus listed loads, give each hidden load a kW value at the summer (16-20h) and winter (17-21h) event hours from the existing L2 block and HDD-slope features, carry the class precision through (L2 precision floor 30.5%), and emit hidden_loads.csv. Person B, about 8 hours: write a rollup.py that takes any meter-to-group CSV. Today it runs on zip. It also runs a clearly labeled sensitivity that groups homes at random into small transformer groups at an assumed kVA rating, and reports the share of groups pushed over rating by recorded load versus recorded plus hidden load. Tag each flagged home with its cheapest fix: managed charging, one battery unit, two units, or a field check. Person C, about 8 hours: add the new numbers to facts.json, add check rules, and build 3 slides: a records-vs-meters gap chart, an asset stress ranking, and the meter-to-transformer CSV schema as the one ask of Avangrid. Also write the limitations: hourly data understates short peaks, and there is no real transformer map.
biggest_risk: The data has no transformer or feeder mapping, so any transformer-level overload count rests on synthetic groupings and assumed kVA ratings. Judges may read that as speculation. The hidden-load counts also carry real classifier error: the L2 precision floor is 30.5% and heat-pump detection is low-confidence. Hourly data hides short peaks, so the stress estimates are optimistic.

title: Headroom Ladder: cheapest fix per home
problem: Avangrid's battery program loses money if it is sold as peak shaving: the batteries take 23 to 33 years to pay back, and their warranty lasts 15. Meanwhile almost every home that adds a Level 2 charger breaks the 3 kVA rule. The utility has no per-home tool that says which fix is cheapest for each home: a thermostat, managed charging, one battery, two batteries, or a full service study.
solution: The tool reads each home's hourly AMI profile and the weather, plus the appliance and segment labels the pipeline already produces. For every home, it simulates the next likely load (a 7.2 kW Level 2 charger, or a heat pump using the computed 0.051 kW per degree F curve). It then tries each fix in order of cost: thermostat setback, managed charging moved into the home's own off-peak hours, one IQ 10C, two IQ 10Cs, and finally a service study. It stops at the first fix that keeps the added load within 3 kVA during event hours. The output is one rung per home, a count of homes and MW on each rung, and a callable check that runs in the 18.6-second ingest pass. The program team and the new-load and interconnection reviewers would use it to approve a request, attach a battery to it, or send it to a study. With that, the battery stops being a blanket peak product and becomes the tool used only where cheaper fixes fail.
decision_changed: It changes how Avangrid targets the BTM BESS program and how it screens new electrification load. Today's draft deploys 8,158 units across 4,079 persistent-peak homes for $73.4M to $106.1M. Under the ladder, thermostats and managed charging handle the homes they can, and batteries go only to homes where a battery is the cheapest way to avoid a service upgrade. title: Filing-Ready Least-Cost Flex Portfolio
problem: Our own numbers show a broad residential battery program cannot be defended at the PSC as a peak-capacity resource: 4,079 candidate homes cost $73.4M to $106.1M and pay back in 23 to 33 years against a 15-year warranty, while a thermostat setback already reaches about 9.9 MW. Regulatory Affairs needs to know which flex resources, at which homes, are cheap enough to justify and recover in NY rates, with every number traceable.
solution: Add a cost-effectiveness and portfolio layer, analysis/bca.py, on top of the existing classify, segment and BESS outputs. Inputs per home are its class flags, segment, coincident summer and winter relief, the 3 kVA headroom result, plus one parameter table of value and cost inputs (capacity $/kW-yr, TOU prices, unit cost, avoided service-upgrade cost), each flagged ASSUMPTION until replaced with NY avoided-cost and tariff values. Method: score each resource (thermostat DR on AC homes, managed charging on EV homes, batteries) by benefit-to-cost ratio and $ per kW. Stack them cheapest first into a least-cost MW supply curve, and keep batteries only where an avoided service upgrade (the electrification-enabled homes) makes the ratio clear 1. Seasonal and inactive homes are excluded. For each battery home it also reports the break-even avoided-upgrade cost, so the conclusion holds whatever the final prices turn out to be. Output: a portfolio table (program, homes, MW summer and winter, cost, ratio), a tornado chart of which assumptions flip the answer, and a ranked customer list. Regulatory Affairs uses it for program filings, Customer Programs for enrollment, and storage policy staff to size the battery pilot.

title: Least-Cost Headroom Ladder
problem: Ranked on peak relief alone, the program battery does not pay back: 23 to 33 years against a 15-year warranty (on assumed prices), and thermostats give peak relief more cheaply. The value lies elsewhere. An unmanaged Level 2 charger breaks the 3 kVA rule at 99.3% of homes, and a battery is what lets those homes electrify without a service study. Avangrid has no per-home way to tell which homes need a battery and which need something cheaper.
solution: The tool takes each home's 8,760-hour AMI load, temperatures and the Part 1 class flags (EV L2, electric heat, AC, seasonal). For every home and every load it might add (a 7.2 kW Level 2 EV, or a heat pump at 0.051 kW per F below 60F), it tests the 3 kVA rule hour by hour. It then picks the cheapest step on a fixed ladder that keeps the home within the rule and still meets the need: thermostat or pool-pump DR, then managed or throttled overnight charging, then one IQ 10C, then two, then a service study. The output is a per-home CSV with columns for the step, kW of headroom, coincident MW and the break-even avoided-upgrade cost. A supply curve shows MW and homes for each step. The Customer Programs and Energy Storage teams would use it to send batteries only where they replace a service upgrade, and Load Forecasting would use it to see where the 5,100 conversions that flip the system to winter-peaking would land. It reuses the existing pipeline, whose ingest takes 18.6 s for 25,653 homes, so it scales to the 3 million-customer base.
decision_changed: BTM BESS program targeting and the service-upgrade screen. Today the battery list is ranked by persistent peak kW, and that list does not pay back. The tool ranks homes by the electrification load that would otherwise trigger a 200 A service study. It covers peak relief with thermostats and managed charging first, which gives about 9.9 MW (33% shed is an assumption) at no hardware cost. A home gets a battery only when the battery is cheaper than the upgrade it avoids. It also lets Avangrid screen the 3 kVA rule from AMI in bulk instead of studying each request.

title: Winter Flip Electrification Stress Test
problem: Nearly every team will tune summer peak shaving, because that is the peak today, and rank batteries by summer peak kW. The meters show that this is temporary. Electric heat is 11.2% of homes but carries 31.9% of winter peak-hour load. Each gas-to-electric heat conversion adds about 3.29 kW at the winter peak, and about 5,100 more conversions would make the system winter-peaking. Avangrid's heat-pump incentives are pushing it toward that flip with no measured trigger.
solution: The build is a scenario engine on top of the existing pipeline that adds measured conversion loads to each home's real 8,760-hour profile. For heat pumps, that is 0.051 kW per degree F below 60F; for Level 2 EVs, it is the observed charging profile. It adds them in the homes most likely to convert, drawn from the emerging, baseline and seasonal segments by Monte Carlo over adoption order. For each adoption count, it reports four things: the system summer and winter peaks, which season sets the peak, how many converting homes break the 3 kVA rule, and how much battery (re-ranked for the 17:00-21:00 winter window) or thermostat capacity keeps the system below today's 59.4 MW peak. The output is a flip curve with an uncertainty band and a 'watch number' of conversions, plus a per-home list that pairs each likely converter with the fix it needs: none, managed charging, one IQ 10C, or two. Load forecasting and load research use the flip curve. Customer programs use the paired list to bundle a heat-pump or EV rebate with storage or load control before the upgrade request arrives.
decision_changed: It changes the battery and demand-response program design decision. The program would target and dispatch for the winter evening peak that electrification creates, not only today's summer afternoon peak. It also turns heat-pump incentive volume into a planning trigger: past roughly the watch number of conversions, each new rebate is paired with load management or storage. In the ranking, the top 1,000 battery homes give 4.43 MW in the winter window against 2.72 MW in summer, so a winter-aware ranking picks different homes and claims more relief per dollar from the same $73.4M to $106.1M capex.

title: Calibrated Appliance Inventory Engine
problem: The pipeline's appliance counts disagree with the population the challenge itself implies. It flags 1,231 heat-pump homes, but the challenge says the 100 listed heat-pump customers are about 25% of the total, so there are about 400 across all 35,725 meters. It flags 1,663 Level 1 and 564 Level 2 EV homes against an implied 560 EV homes. The heat-pump model also finds only 16.7% of the listed heat pumps. Forecasting and program teams cannot plan on an inventory that is off by a factor of about three and has no error bars.
solution: Inputs are the existing 25,653 x 8,760 hourly load matrix, the hourly weather and the three customer lists. Step one is self-supervised pretraining. A small 1D-CNN encoder learns from weekly 168-hour windows of load plus temperature by reconstructing masked hours. It trains on all 223M unlabeled readings, which is where this data's volume is, rather than on the few dozen labeled hits. Each home gets one 64-number embedding. Step two is a positive-unlabeled classifier. It uses the Elkan-Noto correction with the known label frequency c = 0.25 from the challenge statement and runs on the embedding plus the existing hand-built features. This turns scores into true probabilities, so the expected inventory is the sum of the probabilities, with bootstrap intervals. Step three validates the method on solar, the one class with a complete list: hide 75% of the solar list, train the same model, then score it against the full list. Outputs are a per-home probability file, an inventory table that sets rule counts against calibrated counts with intervals, and a precision-at-budget curve. Load Research and Forecasting use the inventory. Customer Programs uses the ranked outreach lists, and the BESS ranking is reweighted to probability x kW relief.
decision_changed: The heating and cooling appliance inventory that Avangrid's load forecasting and electrification program sizing would plan on. Today it is a rule count with no uncertainty (1,231 heat pumps). It becomes a calibrated expected count with an interval that matches the label frequency in the challenge statement. Outreach lists for heat-pump conversion and managed EV charging also change. Today they are yes/no flags. They become lists ranked by probability, with a stated expected hit rate at each mailer budget (for example, the top 500), so a program manager can choose list size by cost per real adopter.

title: Per-Home Heat Pump Load Forecast
problem: The pipeline adds the same 3.29 kW to every home when it estimates what a heat pump conversion does to the winter peak. Gas-heated homes differ widely in size and insulation, so Avangrid cannot tell which conversions it can approve without a study and which ones push a feeder toward winter peaking. The brief puts that tipping point at about 5,100 conversions.
solution: We would build a change-point thermal model for each home. It takes the hourly AMI data already loaded (25,653 homes) and the weather series. For each home it fits a PRISM-style model of daily kWh against temperature: one balance point, a heating slope and a cooling slope, all in kW per degree F, found by grid search and vectorized across all homes. The cooling slope stands in for how leaky the house is. A transfer rule, fitted and cross-validated on the electric-heat homes, where both slopes can be measured, turns it into the heating load the home would have, and a heat pump efficiency curve that falls with temperature turns that into added kW at the 2.1F design day. The output is one line per home that an engineer can check: balance point, the two slopes, predicted added heat pump kW at the design temperature, pass or fail against the 3 kVA rule, and whether one or two IQ 10C units fix a fail. A system roll-up replaces the flat 3.29 kW and 5,100-home figures with an adoption curve that has error bars. Customer Programs uses the per-home list to pick heat pump targets. Load Forecasting and Reliability use the roll-up to see when the system starts peaking in winter.
decision_changed: The decision is which homes Avangrid recruits first for heat pump conversion, and which conversions get through without a service study. Today the 3,573 'emerging' homes are marketed as one undifferentiated group, and every conversion counts as 3.29 kW. With this model, the program goes to the homes with the smallest predicted winter kW first, and batteries or weatherization go only to homes whose predicted load fails the 3 kVA rule. Planners get a winter-peak flip point and a date range they can audit, so they can plan on it instead of resting a call on one average.

At placeholder prices, though, batteries pay back in 23 to 33 years, while cheap thermostat shed covers 9.9 MW. A battery-first list overspends.
solution: A planner workbench on top of the existing pipeline. Inputs: each home's class probabilities, segment, 3 kVA headroom result and its MW contribution in the summer and winter event windows. These come from the pipeline, along with editable price assumptions. Method: a greedy merit-order fill. Every home-lever pair (thermostat shed, one IQ 10C, two units) gets a cost per kW. The tool fills the planner's MW target cheapest-first for the chosen season. Battery offers are restricted to homes where storage does a job a thermostat cannot: it clears the 3 kVA screen for an EV or heat pump, or covers a non-AC winter peak. Output: a supply curve with the target line, a $ cost and $/kW for the portfolio, and an exportable enrollment list showing each home's lever, confidence and the evidence behind it. The users are the Customer Programs manager and the load forecasting director, who use it when sizing a DR or BESS filing.

With the workbench the planner meets the same MW with thermostats first. Batteries go only where they enable electrification or cover winter peak. Season targeting also changes: winter top-1000 homes yield more MW than summer.

title: Firm-MW VPP Portfolio Builder
problem: The pipeline's 14.86 MW battery figure adds up every candidate's relief with perfect foresight, and it sits beside a separate 9.9 MW thermostat number. Avangrid cannot file, fund or dispatch either one as capacity. A VPP operator needs one figure: how many MW the combined fleet will reliably deliver at the event hour in each season, and which resource to buy next.
solution: Inputs are the existing per-home outputs: bess_candidates.csv, customer_classes.csv (AC, pool, EV L2, electric heat), the hourly load matrix and weather. Method: for each top-load day, simulate a day-ahead VPP dispatch with no perfect foresight. The trigger comes from the prior day's temperature forecast. Each battery runs with state of charge, 7.68 kW and 20.16 kWh limits across the 4-hour window and back-to-back event days. Thermostat setback, pool-pump timers and managed EV charging are layered on, each from that home's own counterfactual hourly load. The tool reports P90 "firm" MW for summer and winter, plus a merit-order supply curve in $ per firm kW-yr, with every price flagged as an assumption. The Customer Programs and Energy Storage teams use it to choose the program mix and the battery count where the curve's knee falls.
decision_changed: It changes how many batteries Avangrid funds, which homes get them and which flex program comes first. The current story is a battery at all 4,079 candidates, at $73.4M to $106.1M in capex. The portfolio view would likely show thermostats and pool timers covering the summer peak more cheaply, while batteries earn their place as the winter and electrification hedge. That points the battery program at fewer homes, led by the T1 electrified peakers, where winter MW exceeds summer MW and the 3 kVA headroom pays. Thermostat DR would launch first for the 17,556 AC homes.

title: Charger Watch: meter-found EV enablement
problem: Level 2 chargers are arriving on homes the utility does not know about, and nearly every one breaks the 3 kVA rule. The utility's only answer in the brief is a two-battery setup that takes 23 to 33 years to pay back, yet nobody has tested whether simply moving the charging to other hours would keep the same homes inside 3 kVA for far less money.
solution: Inputs: the hourly AMI matrix the pipeline already loads, the existing EV L2 detector and the EV list. Step one is a change-point pass on each L2 home's daily charging blocks. It dates the first Level 2 day, splitting chargers that were already there from ones that appeared during the year, which gives a meter-measured adoption rate for each month. Step two runs a managed-charging envelope test for every L2 home and for every home that could add a charger. Hour by hour, the cap is the home's own peak plus 3 kVA minus what the home is already drawing, and the test asks whether a 7.2 kW charger, throttled to fit under that cap, can still deliver a night's charge. The result is a third pass rate to set beside the existing ones: no mitigation 0.7%, one IQ 10C 56.6%, two units 100%. Output: a ranked, per-customer routing table (managed charging and EV time-of-use rate / one battery / two batteries / engineering study) plus a ZIP-level count of new chargers. Customer Programs uses it to offer enrollment, and Reliability and Forecasting use it to see where unreported load is growing.
decision_changed: The decision is which enablement offer a home that adds a Level 2 charger gets, and who is told about it. Today the brief's default is two batteries per home, at an assumed $73.4M to $106.1M in capital for the candidate set. After this tool, managed charging plus an EV time-of-use rate goes first to every home whose hourly envelope passes. Batteries go only to homes that fail the envelope and pass with one or two units. Study flags go to the rest, and any newly detected unlisted charger triggers an outreach and planning flag instead of waiting for the customer to say anything.

title: Winter Flip Planner
problem: Avangrid's heat-pump marketing will push this system into winter peaking, and nobody can see it coming. The pipeline's segment table says to market heat pumps to the 3,573 "emerging" homes. Most of those homes heat with something other than electricity today, so each conversion adds about 3.29 kW at the winter peak. About 5,100 conversions would make the system winter-peaking. The utility also can't tell which electric-heat homes already run heat pumps and which still use resistance heat (AUC 0.718), so it doesn't know where a retrofit would cut the winter peak and where a new conversion would add to it.
solution: The tool reads the existing hourly AMI matrix, weather and per-home classes. For every home it measures how winter load responds to cold: kW at the 100 coldest hours minus mild nights, and kW per degree below 60F. From that it estimates each home's winter-peak change under two moves. The first is gas-to-heat-pump, which adds load and is calibrated to the pipeline's 3.29 kW. The second is resistance-to-heat-pump, measured as the gap between listed heat-pump homes and resistance-style homes at the coldest hours, with a bootstrap interval. A scenario engine (Python plus an Excel model for the repo) takes yearly conversion counts by segment and projects winter peak MW against the 59.4 MW summer peak. It returns the conversion count at which the system flips, how far each lever pushes that point back (resistance retrofits, the winter battery tier, keeping seasonal homes out), and a ranked "electrify next" list that puts the conversions with the least winter-peak cost first, each checked against the 3 kVA rule. The users are the load forecasting team, who get the flip point as a forecast input, and customer programs, who get the ordered recruitment list.
decision_changed: It changes the heat-pump program's recruitment order and the winter forecast. Today the pipeline would market heat pumps to the emerging segment first, which uses up the 16.8 MW of winter headroom fastest. The planner would recruit in this order instead: resistance-heat homes first, if the measured retrofit saving holds up; then gas homes, ordered by smallest added winter kW. Gas conversions beyond a set count would be paired with winter DR or a battery. Load forecasting would also get a dated tipping point (about 5,100 conversions, 19.9% of homes, today) to plan winter capacity against.

title: Who Pays, Who Benefits Lens
problem: The battery program as ranked today would spend $73.4M to $106.1M of capital on 4,079 homes (15.9%) and pay back in 23 to 33 years, past the 15-year warranty. Nobody has checked which customers get the bill savings, which ones carry the cost, or which high-bill homes, such as those with electric resistance heat, no program reaches at all. A regulator or a customer-programs manager cannot defend a program portfolio without that check.
solution: The tool is a per-customer bill-impact and program-routing engine built on the existing hourly matrix and class/segment outputs. For every home it computes the annual bill on a flat rate and on TOU (sourced NYSEG/RG&E tariffs replace the assumption.* prices), its winter bill spike, and the bill and peak effect of each program option. The options are a thermostat setback (33% shed assumption), the battery dispatch bess.py already models, managed EV charging, and resistance-to-heat-pump conversion. It then adds the results up by segment into a who-pays/who-benefits ledger: each segment's share of homes, of program capital, of MW relief and of bill savings. It also flags two groups. One is homes that would lose money under a default TOU rate and have no flexible load to shift. The other is high-kWh electric-heat homes that the battery ranking skips. Both are routed to weatherization or heat-pump programs. The output is customer_bills.csv and three deck slides, used by the Customer Programs and Regulatory Affairs NY judges to choose a program mix they can defend in a rate case.
decision_changed: It changes Avangrid's program portfolio decision. Today the default is a battery-first rollout to the highest-load homes. The tool supports leading with thermostats (9.9 MW, assumed 33% shed) as the cheap, broad-reach relief. Batteries go only where they avoid a service upgrade or reach an underserved high-bill segment, and electric-heat homes get winter-specific weatherization and heat-pump offers. It also tells the regulatory team which customers a default TOU rollout would hurt before anyone files it.

title: Upgrade-Avoidance Ladder for Electrification
problem: The battery program does not pay back as a peaker: payback is 23 to 33 years on assumed prices, and thermostats already deliver 9.9 MW of relief more cheaply. Its real value is avoiding a service or transformer upgrade when a home adds an EV charger or heat pump, yet nothing tells a planner which homes need a battery, which need only managed charging, and which need a study.
solution: Build a per-home non-wires screen on top of the existing headroom rule. It takes each home's 8,760-hour load, the pipeline's appliance classes, and a planned added load (unmanaged 7.2 kW Level 2 charger, or heat pump at 0.051 kW per F below 60F). For each home it tries the cheapest option first and stops at the first that keeps added peak load within the 3 kVA rule: no action, then software-only managed charging (limit or shift the charger into hours where the home has room, checked to still deliver the needed daily kWh), then one IQ 10C, then two, and only after that a service-upgrade study. Since the data has no upgrade costs, the output is a break-even number for each home: the avoided-upgrade cost at which a battery beats the wires option, using the brief's capex and value assumptions. The planner compares it to the utility's own upgrade cost. Customer programs staff use the ladder to route homes. Distribution planners get the per-home list plus an optional join on a transformer-ID column, so the same screen covers transformers once Avangrid supplies the map.
decision_changed: It changes how the BESS program targets homes. Today homes are ranked by peak relief, a measure on which thermostats win. Under this screen a battery goes only to homes where electrification would otherwise trigger an upgrade and managed charging cannot avoid it. Homes that managed charging can fix are sent to a cheap managed-charging offer instead. Approving a battery becomes a non-wires-alternative decision: battery cost against the planner's known upgrade cost.

title: Headroom: meter-based load-add screening
problem: When a customer adds a Level 2 charger or heat pump, Avangrid can't tell from its records whether the 200 A service can take it. As a result it either orders an engineering study and service upgrade, or it misses load it never heard about. The battery program is currently pitched as peak relief, where it loses to thermostats: on assumed prices it pays back in 23 to 33 years against a 15-year warranty. Its real value is avoiding those upgrades, and nothing in Avangrid's process captures that today.
solution: Headroom is a screening engine that answers one question per home: "can this home add this load, and what is the cheapest way to make it fit?" Inputs are the home's 8,760 hourly AMI readings, weather, the Part 1 classes (which homes already have EV L2, electric heat or solar) and a standard added-load profile: a 7.2 kW L2 charger, or a heat pump drawing 0.051 kW per degree F below 60 F. It replays the year with the new load and checks it against the 3 kVA rule. It returns the first rung on a ladder that passes: pass as-is, pass with managed charging (charging moved out of the home's own peak hours), pass with 1 IQ 10C, pass with the 2-unit program setup, or needs a study. Each answer comes with a confidence band for how much hourly data hides short peaks. The tool runs on every home for proactive targeting and on single homes for incoming rebate or load-letter requests. The buyer and user is Avangrid customer programs and distribution engineering, who would pay per meter per year once a pilot proves the verdicts match engineering studies.
decision_changed: This changes two Avangrid decisions. First, who gets offered the program battery. Today the default is a ranking by peak kW. Headroom ranks instead by homes where the battery is the cheapest rung that clears an electrification request that would otherwise need a service study or upgrade. Pure peak relief goes to thermostats, which deliver about 9.9 MW on an assumed 33% shed. Second, which load-add requests skip a study. Homes that pass as-is or with managed charging are pre-cleared, so engineering time goes only to the homes the meter says are tight.

title: Least-Cost Flex Offer Ranker
problem: Avangrid has many possible offers (thermostat demand response, a two-battery BESS, managed EV charging, a service upgrade) and no per-home way to pick the cheapest one that delivers the peak relief or electrification each home needs. On our own numbers, a battery bought only for peak shaving takes longer to pay back than its warranty lasts, so offering batteries blanket-style would waste the program budget.
solution: The inputs are the existing pipeline outputs: hourly AMI features, per-class flags with their model scores, segments, battery sizing, and the 3 kVA headroom test. All price inputs come from the facts.json assumption.* keys and are labeled as assumptions. For every home the tool works out the kW each offer would deliver at the summer and winter event windows. It scales that kW by our confidence in the home's appliance class (the positive-unlabeled score or recall) and costs it at $/kW. It then gives the home one action: thermostat first, battery where the home fails the 3 kVA rule for an EV or heat pump (the battery stands in for a service upgrade), battery for pure peak relief only when it beats the thermostat, or no offer. The output is a ranked customer_actions.csv, a cost-ordered MW supply curve that stacks the offers, and an Excel model where judges can change the assumed prices and watch the stack re-sort. The Customer Programs and Storage teams would use it to pick enrollment targets, and Load Forecasting would use it for planning.
decision_changed: It changes the battery program's targeting and its value case. Today the default would be to market the two-battery IQ 10C setup to the 4,079 homes with the highest persistent peaks as a peak-shaving resource. The tool instead puts thermostats first to cover summer peak, sends batteries to homes where they enable an EV charger or heat pump without a service upgrade, and limits pure peak-shave batteries to the top of the supply curve. The same ranking gives the Regulatory Affairs director a filing-ready claim with confidence levels attached: measured peak reduction per offer, which House Rpt 116-474 says the law asks for.
evidence: Battery simple payback is 23 to 33 years (bess.simple_payback_low_yr, bess.simple_payback_high_yr, both on assumed prices), against the 15-year program warranty in the Challenge Statement.

A thermostat setback across AC homes gives 9.9 MW (flex.thermostat_mw, with assumption.thermostat_shed_pct = 33%), compared with 14.86 MW of summer relief from batteries at 4,079 homes (bess.capacity_relief_mw, bess.candidates.count).

An unmanaged Level 2 charger breaks the 3 kVA rule at 99.3% of homes that lack one (bess.headroom_rule.ev_fail_pct_none). One IQ 10C fixes 56.6% of them and two fix 100% (bess.headroom_rule.ev_pass_pct_one_unit, bess.headroom_rule.ev_pass_pct_two_units).

The supply curve has diminishing returns: the top 1,000 homes give 2.72 MW and the top 2,000 give 6.49 MW in summer, out of 14.86 MW from all candidates (bess.supply_curve.top1000_summer_mw, bess.supply_curve.top2000_summer_mw).

Class confidence is uneven, so relief has to be confidence-weighted: solar recall is 91.1% (class.solar.recall_heldout), heat pump PU AUC is 0.718 with 16.7% held-out recall (class.heat_pump.pu_auc, class.heat_pump.recall_heldout), and EV PU AUC is 0.79 (class.ev.pu_auc).
build_plan_24h:
The work splits across three people over about 24 hours.

Person A (analytics, about 10 hours) adds analysis/offers.py on top of bess.py and classify.py. For each home it computes event-window kW for each offer: thermostat at flex.reduction_kw per AC home, battery from the existing sizing, and the electrification-enabling flag from the headroom test. It weights each kW by class confidence and costs it with the assumption.* keys. It assigns one action per home, writes customer_actions.csv and a stacked, cost-ordered supply curve, and adds every new number to facts.json so the trace check still passes.

Person B (deck, about 10 hours) rebuilds the deck in rubric order: problem, data and its defect, classification with recall and confidence intervals, segments by who carries the peak, then the offer stack chart as the centerpiece, the value and payback table, scale, and next steps. Each rubric sub-bullet gets a footer tag so judges can find it.

Person C (rigor and scale, about 8 hours) builds the Excel twin of the offer stack with editable price cells. They run a sensitivity table on capacity $/kW-yr and unit cost, showing which offer wins at which price. They write a scale slide from scale.ingest_seconds (18.6 s) and scale.matrix_gb (1.25 GB) as a measured per-home cost extrapolated to 3 million customers, and they run the repo's self-checks.

The last 2 hours are a joint review that scores the deck against the rubric.
biggest_risk: The value of an avoided service upgrade, which carries the battery case, is not in our data or our cited sources. It has to be shown as an explicit assumption with a break-even ("the battery wins if an upgrade costs more than $X"), not as a measured number. The deck also has to say clearly that the 22,346 electrification-enabled homes are a potential count, not enrollment, or a Load Research judge will distrust every other number.
